claims.claim: Gregory Thaumaturgus, also known as Gregory of Neocaesarea, was a Christian bishop of the 3rd century, born c. 213 in Neocaesarea, Pontus (modern-day Niksar, Turkey) and died c. 270.
Gregory Thaumaturgus was surnamed 'Thaumaturgus' from the Greek for 'miracle-worker' and was canonized as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
Gregory studied law and rhetoric before spending approximately five years (probably 233–238) as a disciple of Origen at Caesarea in Palestine, where he was converted to Christianity.
On returning to Neocaesarea, Gregory was made bishop of his native city and committed his life to Christianizing that largely pagan region.
The work 'On the Vanity of Idols' argues that idols are not gods, that God is one, and that through Christ salvation is given to believers.
In 'On the Vanity of Idols,' the writer shows that those in whose honor temples were founded, statues modelled, victims sacrificed, and festal days celebrated were kings and men and not gods.
The treatise also argues that the power of the Roman Empire was to be attributed to fate rather than to the gods, inasmuch as it had arisen by a certain good fortune.
Gregory Thaumaturgus's surviving theological writings are in an incomplete state, and his pastoral work is but little known.
Gregory participated in the first Synod of Antioch (c. 264), which condemned Paul of Samosata.

During the Decian persecution (250–251), Gregory and his community withdrew into the mountains, and with the return of normal conditions he instituted liturgical celebrations honoring the Decian martyrs.
